title: Ang 157–175: the third and fourth Gurus
hookLine: Guru Amar Das and Guru Ram Das in Gauri
tomorrow: what can't a palace give you, says the fifth Guru?

cards: A song you love turns up twice: once on the album, once on a playlist someone made for bedtime. Simran knows that feeling now.
Every night her dad says the Sohila, the short night prayer, and she's heard one line through the wall since she was small: the body is a town crowded with lust and anger.
Last night, reading Gauri in order, she found the same hymn on Ang 171, under a heading that says Mahala 4. The fourth Guru. But the last line is signed Nanak.
Same hymn, two places, and a fourth Guru signing as the first.

teach.b: Two clues solve it. The first is the heading. In the Granth, the Gurus who wrote hymns sign them Nanak; Sikhs speak of one light passing from Guru to Guru.

teach.h: THE NUMBER IS IN THE HEADING.
teach.b: So the heading carries the number. Mahala 1 is Guru Nanak, Mahala 3 Guru Amar Das, Mahala 4 Guru Ram Das. One name in the signature, the number up top.
The second clue is the Sohila.
The night prayer gathers a few hymns from the raga sections, so when you read the Granth in order, you meet them again at home. That's what happened on Ang 171.
This stretch, Ang 157 to 175, is where the third and fourth Gurus take their turns. Guru Amar Das comes first, in Gauri Guarayri, with hymns on the Word and the restless mind. Then Guru Ram Das.
His hymn, in paraphrase: the town of the body is crowded with lust and anger; meeting the holy, they're broken to pieces. He's not describing a monster.
He's describing an ordinary busy heart, the kind that snaps at the people helping it. The cure he names is company: the holy, the Guru, the Name.
Two Gurus, one signature, and the night prayer, found in daylight.

how: Sikhs say the Sohila at night before sleep; its hymns, including Guru Ram Das's 'town crowded with lust and anger', also stand in their raga sections of the Granth, and every hymn's heading names its raga and its Mahala.

o: a page of the night prayer, printed apart from the Granth
the opening page of Guru Ram Das's own separate book
the page where the third and fourth Gurus' Gauri hymns begin

games.q: who's who in the heading — tap the pairs.
p: the night prayer, its hymns found again

s: a hymn signed Nanak was always written by Guru Nanak
the Gurus who wrote all sign as Nanak; the Mahala number in the heading tells you who.
the Sohila's hymns also appear in their raga sections
Guru Ram Das's town crowded with anger sits on Ang 171, in Gauri.
the town in the hymn is a real city of the Gurus' time
it's the body, and an ordinary busy heart.

games.q: your cousin finds a hymn signed Nanak and says, "cool, Guru Nanak wrote this one." the heading says Mahala 3. what do you tell him?
o: it's Guru Amar Das: the Gurus all sign as Nanak, and the number says who.
he's right: the signature is the author, and Mahala is just the tune.
nobody can know; the Granth never says who wrote which hymn.
games.why: one name in the signature, the number in the heading: Mahala 3 is Guru Amar Das. Sikhs speak of one light passing from Guru to Guru.

practice: Listen for the quietest sound in the room: a fan, a fridge, your own breath. Stay with it the way you'd listen to someone singing in the next room, not fixing anything.
When the mind wanders off to a fight or a list, let the small sound bring you home.
